title: C-Spine & CT Head Decision Rules
sources: Critical Vector — NEXUS, Canadian C-Spine, CT Head & New Orleans Rules (verified against derivation/validation studies, July 2026)
Stiell IG et al. JAMA 2001 (Canadian C-Spine Rule); NEJM 2003 (CCR vs NEXUS head-to-head)
Stiell IG et al. Lancet 2001 (Canadian CT Head Rule); JAMA 2005 (CCHR vs NOC head-to-head)
Haydel MJ et al. NEJM 2000 (New Orleans Criteria)

changelog.change: Initial entry — converted from the CV decision-rules guide. Comparative context for the NEXUS calculator: the four rules, the two head-to-head trials, structural reasons for the performance gap, and the exclusions.

summary: Four validated ways to skip imaging after blunt trauma. Spine: NEXUS (flat 5-item checklist) vs Canadian C-Spine Rule (3-tier, adds range-of-motion). Head: Canadian CT Head Rule (2-tier) vs New Orleans Criteria (flat 7-item). Within each pair the tiered rule is more specific — fewer scans at comparable sensitivity — at the cost of complexity and stricter enrollment.

body.text: Cervical injury and clinically important brain injury after blunt trauma are uncommon relative to how often they're worried about (~2–5% of imaged patients for the spine, single digits for the head). None of the four rules apply to obtunded, intubated, or uncooperative patients, or > 48 h after injury. The interactive NEXUS calculator is a separate module; this reference is the comparative context.

Clear the c-spine without imaging if ALL five are absent: no posterior midline cervical tenderness · normal alertness · no intoxication · no focal neurologic deficit · no painful distracting injury. Sensitivity 99.6%, specificity 12.9%. No formal age cutoff (theoretically all ages > 1 y). Low specificity is the price of simplicity — any one positive criterion mandates imaging.
For alert (GCS 15), haemodynamically stable trauma patients only. Three-tier tree:

items: Step 1 — high-risk factors (any one → image): age ≥ 65, dangerous mechanism (fall ≥ 3 ft / 5 stairs, axial load to head, high-speed MVC, rollover, ejection, motorized recreational vehicle, bicycle collision), or paresthesias in the extremities.

Step 2 — if no high-risk factor, a low-risk factor allows range-of-motion testing: simple rear-end MVC, sitting position in the ED, ambulatory at any point since injury, delayed onset of neck pain, absence of midline C-spine tenderness.
Step 3 — range of motion: if the patient can actively rotate the neck 45° left AND right, no imaging. If not — or if no low-risk factor is present — image.

body.text: Sensitivity 100% (derivation), specificity 42.5%. Excludes penetrating trauma, known vertebral disease, pregnancy, acute paralysis; age ≥ 65 is itself an automatic imaging trigger.
Head-to-head (Stiell, NEJM 2003 — 8,283 patients, same physicians applied both)

Both differences significant (P < 0.001). CCR caught more injuries AND ordered fewer scans. The gap is structural, not one rule being 'smarter': NEXUS is a flat checklist with no discrimination once tenderness or distraction is present; CCR adds a functional test (active ROM) for the intermediate group, releasing more true negatives without missing true positives. Cost: CCR takes longer to learn and apply, and ROM testing on a trauma patient makes some clinicians uneasy.

NEXUS in the elderly: sensitivity drops in patients > 65 — as low as 66–84% in some cohorts (99.6% overall); a 231,018-patient retrospective study still held it at 94.8%. Picture is mixed — caution warranted either way. 'Distracting injury' and 'intoxication' are not rigidly defined in NEXUS, which is part of why its specificity is so low (inter-clinician variation).
Head — minor head injury (witnessed LOC, definite amnesia, or witnessed disorientation)
Canadian CT Head Rule (Stiell, Lancet 2001 — 3,121 patients, GCS 13–15)

items: High-risk (any one → predicts need for neurosurgical intervention, mandates CT): GCS < 15 at 2 h after injury · suspected open or depressed skull fracture · any sign of basal skull fracture (hemotympanum, raccoon eyes, CSF oto-/rhinorrhea, Battle's sign) · ≥ 2 episodes of vomiting · age ≥ 65.

Medium-risk (added on top; any one → predicts clinically important brain injury on CT): amnesia before impact > 30 min · dangerous mechanism (pedestrian struck, occupant ejected, fall > 3 ft or 5 stairs).

body.text: Excludes age < 16, anticoagulated patients (in the original derivation), obvious open skull fracture, seizure before assessment, and return visits for the same injury.
New Orleans Criteria (Haydel, NEJM 2000 — 520 derivation / 909 validation, GCS 15 + normal neuro exam)

Flat checklist — any one present → CT: headache · vomiting (any episode) · age > 60 · drug or alcohol intoxication · persistent anterograde amnesia (short-term memory deficit) · physical evidence of trauma above the clavicles · seizure. Sensitivity 100% in original cohorts (pooled 97.2–98.3%); specificity ~25% derivation (pooled 8.5–12.3%). 'Headache' and 'vomiting' alone flag a large share of any minor-head-injury population — NOC trades specificity for a hard-to-miss checklist.

rows: Broader pooled (14 studies, 21,140 pts) — sensitivity for clinically important brain injury

body.text: Both caught every case that mattered for neurosurgery; the entire practical difference is specificity — CCHR sends far fewer people to CT for the same safety margin. NOC's extra sensitivity in the broader estimate comes at a steep specificity cost. CCHR excludes anticoagulated and pediatric patients; NOC does not carry those exclusions, which is part of why it's still reached for.

rows: Which spine rule catches more injuries?
Which head rule catches more for neurosurgery?
Tied at 100%, but CCHR is far more specific (76.3% vs 12.1%)
NOC — a flat 7-item checklist; CCHR needs the 2-tier structure
Which rules work in obtunded patients?
None — all require an alert, cooperative exam
CCR and CCHR treat ≥ 65 as an automatic imaging trigger; NOC uses > 60; NEXUS has none formally

Alert, stable, cooperative patient: CCR for the neck, CCHR for the head — a little less simplicity for meaningfully fewer scans. NEXUS and NOC are reasonable faster fallbacks when the Canadian rules' enrollment criteria aren't met.
